newsitem.title: USA: Gorbachev says Yeltsin potential exhausted.
newsitem.headline: Gorbachev says Yeltsin potential exhausted.

text.p: Former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev said on Thursday that he was calling on Russian President Boris Yeltsin to resign because he had "exhausted his potential" both physically and politically.
Speaking to reporters in San Francisco, Gorbachev reiterated the call for Yeltsin's resignation that he first made in interviews with Russian media last week.
"I am not only calling today. I did call upon him to resign and then the political process should take its course according to the constitution," Gorbachev said.
Gorbachev said he wished Yeltsin, who has heart problems, a quick recovery but he believed that "both physically and politically the president has exhausted his potential."
"He (Yeltsin) has not been actually working for a few months and ... the country is for all practical purposes without a functioning president," Gorbachev said.
Yeltsin has been in a Moscow hospital since Sept. 13 and faces a heart bypass operation in six to 10 weeks. Yeltsin, 65, assured Russians on Thursday that he was still in charge of the country.

Gorbachev said that, if Yeltsin stepped down, the prime minister would take over his functions and new elections would be held in three months. "Who will be elected by the Russian voters is a question to be answered by them," Gorbachev said.
Gorbachev, last president of the Soviet Union, was one of several candidates who ran against Yeltsin in the first round of Russia's presidential election this year but he won few votes.

Gorbachev said that, as a Soviet Politburo member for seven years, he had seen how the illnesses of a succession of Soviet leaders, including Leonid Brezhnev, Yuri Andropov and Konstantin Chernenko, had made decision-making difficult.
Gorbachev also said he thought it would be a bad idea for countries such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join NATO.

"I don't think that Russia would declare war on others if some countries would become members of NATO. That's out of the question. But certainly Russia would draw certain political and military conclusions. I don't know what kind of conclusions, but there definitely will be certain countersteps and do we need all this?" he asked.

The former Soviet leader is attending the "State of the World Forum," a five-day conference of politicians, business executives, scientists and religious figures from around the world to discuss social and economic problems.
